newsitem.title: UK: Precious Outlook - Gold poised for new decline.
newsitem.headline: Precious Outlook - Gold poised for new decline.

text.p: The precious metals appeared poised to crumble further after taking a beating last week which shaved $5.00 from the price of gold, dealers said.

"Both silver and gold are at critical levels right now," one said. "Gold is right on $377-$378 an ounce and silver is at $4.80, which are considered the last stops on the line before entering unconsidered territory."
Gold finished last week at $377.40/$377.90 an ounce in London after coming under heavy pressure from sales linked to speculators and gold producers.
But a bounce from this critical support area was possible considering the market's oversold condition, some analysts said.
The behaviour of Australian producers might hold the key for near-term prices, with continued selling seen possibly breaching support, Dresdner bank said in a weekly report.
"(Producers) have been panicky, waiting for shorts to cover and now that we're under $380 they could wave the white flag and just sell anyway. That's what the market fears," a dealer said.
Funds, already short of the market, were unlikely to start covering with sentiment as bearish as it was, he added.
A spike in near-term gold lease rates, notably three-month rates, also raised the possibility of further producer selling in the coming months, dealer said.
One-month lease rates were at 2.52 percent on Friday, up from 1.89 at the start of last week. Three-month rates were at 2.59 percent, higher than both six- and 12-month rates.

Widespread rumours of possible central bank sales also helped set the bearish tone. A report from investment bank SBC Warburg said Euroepan nations keen to join the first wave of European Monetary Union (EMU) might be tempted to sell gold reserves early next year to meet EMU rules on their debt levels.
Such sales were likely to depress the price of gold, said Stephen York, Warburg director of the political research.
"As we near the early-1998 EMU assessment period the temptation for some countries to raid their gold reserves to reduce debt in 1997 may be overwhelming," the report said.
Bad news for bulls also came in the form of U.S. economic news last week which indicated recent inflation fears were unfounded. "All the news is bearish," a dealer said.
The other precious metals were also balancing on the edge of key support levels and eyeing gold for future direction.
Silver ended last week at $4.77/$4.79 an ounce, which if decisively breached on the downside targeted $4.70 and possibly further declines toward $4.50 an ounce.
Platinum, caught between ample supplies and lacklustre demand, tumbled about $4.00 to finish Friday at $379.50/$380.50 an ounce.
"If gold goes, platinum may follow it, although it's been marked up and down recently in a $379.50-$382.50 range," a dealer said.
Palladium was stuck in the same bind and was hovering just above its $115.00 support level. A breach pointed to $112.
